cim: News - The hidden risks of the artificial intelligence supply chain
cim_eredeti: News - The hidden risks of the artificial intelligence supply chain
szoveg_eredeti:
As businesses accelerate their adoption of artificial intelligence, many are acquiring technologies whose underlying infrastructure they have little visibility over. An application purchased from a single vendor may depend on external model providers, open-source software, third-party datasets, cloud infrastructure and a growing number of integrations with other business systems.

Each of these dependencies introduces potential security weaknesses, some of which may sit several layers beyond an organisation’s direct commercial relationships.

Research published on 10 November by third-party risk intelligence firm Black Kite identified widespread security weaknesses among companies developing, deploying and supporting artificial intelligence technologies.

Among its findings, researchers identified 1,732 security issues across publicly discoverable components using Model Context Protocol, a technology that allows artificial intelligence applications to interact with external tools and business systems.

The findings come at a time when organisations are increasingly allowing these applications to access sensitive corporate information, communicate with external services and carry out tasks previously performed by employees. The security implications of a compromised supplier consequently become more significant as these applications assume greater operational responsibilities.

Traditional third-party risk management programmes generally involve assessing a supplier’s security practices, reviewing its certifications and establishing contractual obligations around data protection and incident reporting. Applying the same approach to artificial intelligence can become complicated when the supplier itself relies on numerous external technologies.

A business purchasing an automated customer service platform, for example, may have a contractual relationship with the application provider but no direct relationship with the company supplying its underlying language model. The application may also rely on separate services to retrieve customer information, process documents or generate responses.

A security incident affecting any of these providers could have consequences for the purchasing organisation, even if its immediate supplier maintains adequate security controls.

The complexity of these relationships was examined in a report published in March 2026 by the University of Oxford and Plexal. The researchers developed a framework for understanding the artificial intelligence supply chain, examining how security weaknesses can emerge and spread across interconnected systems.

Among the challenges identified were the deliberate manipulation of training data, interference with model components and malicious instructions introduced through external content.

Training data presents a particularly difficult problem. Organisations using pre-trained models may have limited knowledge of the sources from which the data was collected, how it was processed or what measures were taken to protect its integrity.

A model trained on deliberately manipulated data could produce unreliable or harmful results under particular circumstances. Identifying the source of such behaviour may require access to information that the purchasing organisation does not possess.

Similar concerns apply to open-source models and software components. Developers can download existing models, adapt them for particular business purposes and incorporate them into commercial applications. This offers considerable advantages in terms of development costs and accessibility, although establishing the integrity of every component can be difficult.

Security assessments also need to account for what happens after an application has been approved for use. Providers may introduce new models, change infrastructure arrangements or expand their integrations with external services. These changes can alter the organisation’s exposure without necessarily triggering a new procurement or security review.

The emergence of autonomous artificial intelligence agents adds another dimension to the problem. An application that generates internal reports presents a different level of exposure from one that can access employee records, modify databases, communicate with suppliers or authorise transactions.

A compromised component within the latter could have consequences that extend well beyond the application itself. The permissions granted to these systems deserve particular scrutiny, especially where they can perform actions across multiple business environments.

There is also the question of market concentration. Despite the growing number of artificial intelligence products available to businesses, many rely on the same relatively small group of underlying technology providers.

An organisation may believe it has diversified its technology suppliers by purchasing applications from several vendors, only to discover that those applications depend on the same language model or cloud infrastructure.

This creates the potential for widespread disruption following a single security incident or service outage. It also complicates business continuity planning, particularly when alternative providers rely on similar infrastructure.

In its guidance published on 19 November 2026, the Bank of England highlighted the importance of identifying artificial intelligence models, their associated dependencies and the exposures they introduce to important business services.

While the guidance addresses financial institutions, the underlying concerns are relevant to organisations across industries. Businesses need to understand which operations depend on these technologies, what would happen if a provider became unavailable and whether critical functions could continue without them.

Procurement departments have an important role in addressing these risks. Questions about where corporate data is processed, which external providers support an application and how changes to its underlying technology are communicated should form part of supplier assessments.

The UK’s Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI also establishes expectations around secure supply chain practices, placing responsibilities on developers and system operators throughout the technology’s lifecycle.

For businesses, obtaining meaningful assurances from suppliers may prove challenging. Vendors may be reluctant to disclose commercially sensitive information about their infrastructure or may themselves have limited visibility over certain dependencies. Procurement teams will need to determine what level of uncertainty is acceptable, particularly when applications are being introduced into critical business functions.

Security leaders should also consider how an organisation would respond to a compromise affecting an underlying model or software component. Establishing whether an affected technology can be isolated, replaced or temporarily disabled should form part of incident response and business continuity planning.

Much of the commercial discussion surrounding artificial intelligence adoption has centred on productivity, cost savings and competitive advantage. As businesses become more dependent on these technologies, the security and reliability of the companies supporting them deserve greater attention.

Before expanding their use of artificial intelligence, organisations would benefit from establishing a clearer picture of the technologies they already depend on. For many businesses, that exercise may reveal a supply chain considerably larger and more concentrated than their procurement records suggest.
